title: Unsecured Credentials: Shell History
summary: This sub-technique is credential collection from command history, which shells write to disk so a user can review or repeat earlier input. On Linux and macOS the history file for the interactive shell, such as the bash or zsh history in the user's home directory, is flushed when the session ends and by default retains a limited number of recent commands. On Windows, the command prompt keeps no persistent history, but PowerShell writes a cross-session history file under the user's application data folder, and an in-session history is also available through the Get-History cmdlet. The weakness is behavioural: operators pass credentials as command parameters, source secrets from files, and paste connection strings, so the secret is recorded in plaintext beside the command that used it. Detection relies on command-line logging and on file access auditing of those history paths, since a reader other than the interactive user's own shell is anomalous. Retention and history settings are the primary controls.

beginner.definition: A command line asks you to type instructions. Most shells save what you typed in a file so you can look back later. This sub-technique is when an attacker reads that saved list and finds passwords people typed as part of a command.
beginner.whyItMatters: People often type a password straight into a command, for example to connect to a database. That password is then saved in a plain file. The attacker reads the file in seconds and gains access to systems they never had to break into.
howItWorks: A shell keeps a list of the commands you type during your session.
When you log out, that list is written to a file in your home folder.
The file holds your recent commands, usually the last thousand or so.
On Windows, a similar file stores PowerShell commands from all your sessions.
Anyone who can read the file sees passwords typed as command options.
The attacker then reuses those credentials against many other systems and services.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk with a notepad where staff write down each task they complete. Someone writes the cabinet code next to the note about restocking supplies. A visitor waiting at the desk reads the page while nobody is looking. The cabinet was never opened, and the code was never guessed. It was simply written down in an open book.
takeaways: Never type a password directly into a command line.
History files record credentials in plain text and need protection.
Set history limits and clear history where it is not needed.

objectives: Explain what a shell history file is and when it is written.
Describe the difference between Linux, macOS and Windows command history storage.
Explain how a password typed as a command parameter becomes a stored secret.
Identify the log and file access evidence of history file collection.
Describe configuration changes that reduce credentials retained in history.
